:::: model-field-sheet
## Purpose

This model estimates WTA player strength over time and across surfaces, with uncertainty, by treating historical market probabilities as noisy observations of latent player strength. The aim of this model is not to beat today's market, but to use public pricing history to create the most accurate, holistic ranking of tour players available anytime. Current estimates are published on the [WTA Rankings](/tennis/rankings/) page.

The system has two stages which share the same generative model. Each off-season, the global model learns the shared parameters while integrating over the player states. During the season, those parameters are fixed while the online player model estimates latent strengths before each day's matches.

## Data

One row per match: players $i$ and $j$, date $t$, surface $s$, player ages, prior WTA appearances, surface type, and decimal odds $o_{i,m}$ and $o_{j,m}$. These data were acquired for nearly every WTA match from 2019 to 2026.

The odds are converted to raw implied probabilities and de-vigged:

$$
\pi_{i,m}=\frac{1}{o_{i,m}},
\qquad
p_{i,m}=\frac{\pi_{i,m}}{\pi_{i,m}+\pi_{j,m}},
\qquad
y_m=\log\frac{p_{i,m}}{1-p_{i,m}}.
$$

The raw bookmaker margin is $v_m=\pi_{i,m}+\pi_{j,m}-1$. The model uses its training-standardized value,

$$
V_m=\frac{v_m-\bar v_{\mathrm{train}}}{s_{v,\mathrm{train}}}.
$$

The stored odds are the source's first available bookmaker; though bookmaker identity is not preserved, this is almost completely *bet365*. When forecasting a match, its own price is not used: all matches on a date are predicted before prices from that date update the player states. Match outcomes are used only for evaluation.

## States

- $x_{i,t}$ = player $i$'s overall strength at time $t$
- $\mathbf u_i=(u_{i,\mathrm{hard}},u_{i,\mathrm{clay}},u_{i,\mathrm{grass}})$ = player $i$'s surface effects
- $z$ = all player states and surface effects

## Parameters

$\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma)$ denotes a distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$; $\operatorname{Normal}_2(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ uses covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$.

- $\theta$ = all shared system parameters
- $\tau_0$ = population entry SD, in log-odds; $\tau_0\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(1.5,0.75)$
- $\sqrt q$ = process SD, in log-odds per square-root year; $\sqrt q\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(0.5,1)$
- $\sqrt r$ = base observation SD, in log-odds; $\sqrt r\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(0.25,0.75)$
- $\tau_s$ = SD of the orthonormal surface contrasts, in log-odds; $\tau_s\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(0.35,0.75)$
- $\beta_g$ = annual pre-peak growth, in log-odds; $\beta_g\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(0.4,0.75)$
- $\beta_d$ = annual post-peak decline, in log-odds; $\beta_d\sim\operatorname{LogNormal}(0.15,1)$
- $\gamma_e$ = change in log entry SD per standardized unit of prior experience; $\gamma_e\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,0.5)$
- $\gamma_v$ = change in log observation SD per standardized unit of bookmaker margin; $\gamma_v\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,0.5)$

## State model

Player strength at entry is drawn from the tour population:

$$
\log \tau_i=\log\tau_0+\gamma_e E_i,
\qquad
x_{i,1} \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,\tau_i).
$$

$E_i$ is the training-standardized value of $\log(1+n_i)$, where $n_i$ is player $i$'s number of stored WTA appearances before entering the panel.

The live model fixes peak age at 24 and uses the piecewise-linear age path:

$$
a(A;\beta)=
\begin{cases}
\beta_g(A-24), & A<24,\\
-\beta_d(A-24), & A\geq24.
\end{cases}
$$

The peak is an assumption rather than an estimated parameter. Though this isn't rigorous, aging is a minor concern from match-to-match. More work would be needed to create longer-term projections.

Player strength then evolves as:

$$
x_{i,t} \mid x_{i,t-1}
\sim
\operatorname{Normal}\!\left(
x_{i,t-1}+a(A_{i,t};\beta)-a(A_{i,t-1};\beta),
\sqrt{q\Delta t}
\right).
$$

$\Delta t$ is elapsed calendar time in years. The mean follows the age path; variance grows linearly with elapsed time.

Each player has zero-sum random effects for hard, clay and grass. They are represented using two orthonormal Helmert contrasts.

$$
\mathbf c_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}_2(\mathbf 0,\tau_s^2\mathbf I_2),
\qquad
\mathbf u_i=\mathbf C\mathbf c_i,
$$

$$
\mathbf C=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/\sqrt 2 & 1/\sqrt 6\\
-1/\sqrt 2 & 1/\sqrt 6\\
0 & -2/\sqrt 6
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf 1^\mathsf T\mathbf u_i=0.
$$

This is a convenient way to impose $u_{i,\mathrm{hard}}+u_{i,\mathrm{clay}}+u_{i,\mathrm{grass}}=0$ while giving every surface the same prior treatment. Each named surface effect has population SD $\sqrt{2/3}\,\tau_s$; effects for two different surfaces have correlation $-1/2$ because increasing one must be offset by the others.

## Observation model

For match $m$, the expected market log-odds are the difference between the two players' overall strengths and surface effects:

$$
\eta_m
=
x_{i,t}-x_{j,t}+u_{i,s}-u_{j,s},
$$

Observation SD changes with bookmaker margin:

$$
\log\sqrt{r_m}=\log\sqrt r+\gamma_v V_m,
\qquad
y_m \mid z,\theta
\sim
\operatorname{Normal}(\eta_m,\sqrt{r_m}).
$$

$r_m$ determines how strongly the observed price updates the player states.

## Fit

**Off-season global fit**

Let $y_{\mathrm{train}}$ contain the eligible market log-odds from the preceding seasons in a ten-season window. The 2026 fit uses every available season from 2019 through 2025. The shared parameters are estimated by maximum a posteriori probability while the player states are integrated out:

$$
\hat\theta
=
\underset{\theta}{\arg\max}
\left\{
\log\int
p(y_{\mathrm{train}}\mid z,\theta)
p(z\mid\theta)\,dz
+\log p(\theta)
\right\}.
$$

The Gaussian integral is evaluated exactly in sparse precision form; player states are not optimizer coordinates.

**In-season online fit**

Given fitted parameters $\hat\theta$, estimate the player states from prices observed before date $t$:

$$
p(z_t\mid y_{<t},\hat\theta).
$$

Carry the state distributions forward, predict a given set of matches, then condition on the new prices. This is implemented as an information-form Kalman update.

Dynamic player states, filtering and offline parameter estimation are established parts of skill-rating models; [Duffield, Power and Rimella](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssc/article/73/5/1262/7734616) demonstrate that workflow on WTA results. Surface-specific tennis states also appear in [Gorgi, Koopman and Lit](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12464), while [Ingram](https://doi.org/10.1515/jqas-2018-0008) separates serve and return skill using point outcomes. [Leitner, Zeileis and Hornik](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2009.10.001) recover latent ability from bookmaker consensus. Here, de-vigged match prices are the observations, and the linear-Gaussian form allows the player states to be integrated exactly during the global fit.

## Results

The evaluation contains 6,381 matches from the 2024 and 2025 seasons. There are two benchmarks.

1. The market benchmark uses the de-vigged price for the match being predicted.
2. The Elo benchmark initializes every player at 1500, uses the conventional 400-point logistic scale with a fixed $K=32$, and warms up on matches from 2021 through 2023. It maintains one rating across surfaces and uses only outcomes observed before that day.

::: model-field-sheet
The fraction of market signal retained is defined against a coin flip forecast:

$$
S
=
\frac{\operatorname{LL}(0.5)-\operatorname{LL}(\text{model})}
{\operatorname{LL}(0.5)-\operatorname{LL}(\text{market})}.
$$
:::

| Metric | Surface | Matches | Market | Player-state | Elo |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Log loss | **Overall** | **6,381** | **0.581** | **0.597** | **0.628** |
| Log loss | Hard | 3,951 | 0.586 | 0.600 | 0.633 |
| Log loss | Clay | 1,663 | 0.561 | 0.579 | 0.617 |
| Log loss | Grass | 767 | 0.596 | 0.620 | 0.630 |
| Brier score | **Overall** | **6,381** | **0.199** | **0.206** | **0.220** |
| Brier score | Hard | 3,951 | 0.202 | 0.207 | 0.222 |
| Brier score | Clay | 1,663 | 0.191 | 0.199 | 0.215 |
| Brier score | Grass | 767 | 0.206 | 0.216 | 0.220 |
| Signal retained | **Overall** | **6,381** | **100.0%** | **85.4%** | **57.7%** |
| Signal retained | Hard | 3,951 | 100.0% | 86.8% | 56.3% |
| Signal retained | Clay | 1,663 | 100.0% | 85.9% | 57.8% |
| Signal retained | Grass | 767 | 100.0% | 76.1% | 64.9% |

## Validation

The first check asks whether the mean predictions are calibrated. Regressing the observed result on the model log-odds gives an intercept for systematic bias and a slope for whether the predictions vary by the right amount. An intercept of zero and slope of one indicate calibration.

| Subset | Matches | Intercept \[95% interval\] | Slope \[95% interval\] |
|:--------------|--------------:|----------------------:|-------------------:|
| **Overall** | **6,381** | **−0.008 \[−0.065, 0.045\]** | **1.045 \[0.982, 1.116\]** |
| 2024 | 3,167 | −0.020 \[−0.096, 0.052\] | 1.087 \[0.996, 1.178\] |
| 2025 | 3,214 | +0.004 \[−0.074, 0.082\] | 1.007 \[0.912, 1.110\] |
| Hard | 3,951 | −0.016 \[−0.083, 0.054\] | 1.019 \[0.929, 1.109\] |
| Clay | 1,663 | +0.021 \[−0.079, 0.122\] | 1.182 \[1.048, 1.340\] |
| Grass | 767 | −0.019 \[−0.178, 0.144\] | 0.909 \[0.748, 1.069\] |

The second check asks whether the predictive standard deviations are calibrated. The predictive distribution for a market price combines uncertainty in the latent matchup with fitted observation noise. Its standardized innovations should have SD one, and its central intervals should attain their nominal coverage.

| Surface     | Innovation SD | 50% interval | 80% interval | 95% interval |
|:------------|--------------:|-------------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| Hard        |         0.953 |        53.0% |        83.4% |        96.3% |
| Clay        |         0.976 |        52.1% |        81.5% |        95.6% |
| Grass       |         1.121 |        48.1% |        77.4% |        91.9% |
| **Overall** |     **0.981** |    **52.2%** |    **82.2%** |    **95.6%** |

The pooled standardized innovations have mean +0.018. The overall predictive intervals are slightly conservative, while the smaller grass sample is under-dispersed.

As a separate check on player-level uncertainty, 95% intervals for pre-match matchup strength contained 94.5% of subsequent market revisions.

These diagnostics are reproducible using the [evaluation data](/assets/data/wta-model-validation.csv) and [validation script](https://github.com/spazznolo/spazznolo.github.io/blob/master/scripts/wta_validation.py).

## Interpretation

1.  The player-state model retains 85.4% of the market's signal, compared with 57.7% for standard Elo, despite using no information from the match being predicted.
2.  Performance is consistent on hard and clay courts, where the model retains about 86% of market signal. Grass is weaker at 76%, based on a smaller sample of 767 matches.
3.  The mean predictions are well calibrated overall and in both seasons. Clay predictions may be slightly too conservative, while the smaller grass sample remains consistent with either good calibration or modest overconfidence.
4.  Predictive uncertainty is also well calibrated overall. The intervals are slightly conservative on hard and clay courts and too narrow on grass.
5.  Surface effects account for roughly 10% of the spread in player strength. They are useful adjustments to a player's overall level, not separate ratings of comparable size.

The [ranking states](/assets/data/wta-rankings-latest.csv), [surface summary](https://github.com/spazznolo/spazznolo.github.io/blob/master/scripts/wta_surface_dispersion.py), and validation materials reproduce these results.

## Next steps

1.  Separate chronic player strength from an acute form signal to absorb short-term correlation in market innovations.
2.  Evaluate the aging curve with multi-year projections made without intermediate market updates.
3.  Decompose player strength into point-level serve and return states, and revisit calibration on clay and uncertainty on grass.
